plan_a_advantages: Plan A has slightly more total easy running time, which could be beneficial for building a solid aerobic base.
Plan A's focus on form and breathing during easy runs is a good practice for efficiency.
Plan A has a slightly higher number of easy runs, which may be preferable for athletes who are new to training or prone to injury.
plan_b_advantages: Plan B incorporates hill training, which is crucial for trail running speed and strength.
The threshold intensity hill workouts in Plan B will build more power and endurance than Plan A's easy runs.
Plan B's structure is more likely to lead to improvements in trail-specific performance.
Plan B includes a more varied training stimulus, which can help prevent plateaus.
reasoning: While both plans incorporate rest days and easy runs, Plan B is better suited for the goal of becoming a faster trail runner. The inclusion of dedicated hill sessions (twice a week) directly addresses a key element of trail running: climbing efficiently and building leg strength. Plan A focuses solely on easy runs, which, while important for base building and recovery, won't significantly improve speed on varied terrain. The threshold intensity of the hill workouts in Plan B will contribute more effectively to developing the necessary power and endurance for faster trail times.
